h1: The 8 Best Fat Soluble Vitamin B1 Supplements, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Fat Soluble B1 Supplements: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 fat soluble vitamin B1 supplements (benfotiamine and TTFD) scored on dose clarity, form, testing and value.
summary: Pure Encapsulations BenfoMax is the benfotiamine to buy if you want a clean label and a clearly stated 200 mg per capsule. Double Wood is the best pick for split dosing with third-party testing, Nutricost is the best 600 mg value with an NSF-certified, GMP facility, and Nutri TTFD is the choice if you specifically want the TTFD form. Talk to your doctor before starting any of these.
intro: The first mistake people make with fat soluble B1 is comparing bottles by milligrams per capsule. A bottle showing 600 mg may need two or three capsules to reach that dose, a softgel is not the same product as a capsule, and TTFD is a different molecule from benfotiamine with its own dose range. The label that matters is the serving line, not the front of the bottle.

This guide is educational, not medical advice, and it does not tell you what a supplement will do for you. We ranked eight products on form (benfotiamine or TTFD), milligrams per serving, capsules per serving, delivery type, third-party testing, allergen disclosure and value, using the listings and manufacturer statements. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before you start any supplement, especially if you take medication.

products.name: Pure Encapsulations BenfoMax, 90 Capsules, 200 mg Benfotiamine, Vitamin B1 Thiamin Supplement
products.verdict: A single-ingredient benfotiamine with 200 mg per capsule and a short, allergen-aware label.
products.description:
BenfoMax delivers 200 mg of benfotiamine in each of 90 capsules, made from Japanese benfotiamine, in a vegan, non-GMO formula. Pure Encapsulations says it leaves out common allergens, artificial ingredients and unnecessary additives, and states that products are tested to verify potency and purity.

It ranks first because the label is the easiest to read: one dose per capsule, no blend to decode, and a single active. The Double Wood below gives the same split-dose flexibility at a lower price, but it carries 150 mg per capsule, so you take more capsules for a larger serving. The cost of BenfoMax is the price, the top of this ranking at $50 to $100. Choose it if you want a clean label.

Pick it when label simplicity is worth the premium. The caveat is that 90 capsules at 200 mg is a limited supply for anyone taking more than one a day.
products.idealFor: Anyone who wants a minimal label and a simple one-capsule serving.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest cost per milligram.

products.name: Benfotiamine 300mg, Vitamin B1, Fat Soluble, 120 Capsules (Double Wood Supplements)
products.verdict: A 300 mg serving split across two 150 mg capsules, tested for microbes and heavy metals.
products.description:
Double Wood sells benfotiamine as 150 mg capsules, 120 per bottle, so a 300 mg serving is two capsules and the bottle lasts 60 servings. The maker says it is made and tested in the USA for microbes and heavy metals, and that it has been third-party tested. The label is vegetarian-safe.

It ranks second because the split-dose design is genuinely useful: one capsule at lunch and one at dinner is easier than a big single dose, and 150 mg gives you finer control than the 300 mg capsules used by DEAL Supplement. It ranks below BenfoMax only on label minimalism and on the lack of a stated certification such as NSF.

Buy it if you want a moderate serving that you can adjust capsule by capsule. The caveat is a two-month supply, which is shorter than the 90-serving bottles from Nutricost and DEAL.
pros: Tested for microbes and heavy metals
products.idealFor: People who want a moderate serving they can spread across two meals.
products.skipIf: You want a 600 mg serving from fewer capsules.

products.name: Nutricost Benfotiamine (600mg) 180 Capsules, Fat Soluble Vitamin B1, 90 Servings
products.verdict: A 600 mg serving from two capsules, made in an NSF certified, GMP compliant, FDA registered facility.
products.description:
Nutricost provides 600 mg of benfotiamine per serving, with 2 capsules per day for 90 servings from 180 capsules. The bottle is gluten free, GMO free and vegan, and the maker says it is made in an NSF Certified, GMP Compliant, FDA Registered facility.

It ranks third because the facility certification is a stronger quality signal than a general testing claim, and the cost per milligram is low, in the under $30 bracket. It sits below Double Wood because a 600 mg serving offers less flexibility to adjust, and below BenfoMax because it uses a longer inactive list.

Buy it if you have already settled on a 600 mg serving with your clinician and want a long supply. The caveat is that the facility is certified, but the listing does not say that each lot is independently tested, so ask the maker for a certificate of analysis if you care.
products.idealFor: People using 600 mg who want a three-month supply at a low price.
products.skipIf: You prefer smaller capsules you can adjust.

products.name: Life Extension Benfotiamine with Thiamine, 100 mg, 120 Capsules
products.verdict: A low-dose 100 mg capsule from a maker that publishes a certificate of analysis for its products.
products.description:
Life Extension lists 100 mg per capsule in a 120-capsule bottle, with benfotiamine alongside thiamine. The listing says expert formulators design the formulas, that a certificate of analysis is available for every product, and that the majority of products are non-GMO and gluten-free.

It ranks fourth because a 100 mg capsule is a lower dose than the 150 to 300 mg capsules ahead of it, so it suits a cautious start, and the certificate of analysis is the best documentation promise in the group. It loses ground to Nutricost on cost per milligram, since reaching 300 mg takes three capsules.

Buy it for a low-dose, well-documented bottle. The caveat is the value: the listing combines two B1 forms, so check the Supplement Facts panel for the exact amounts of each before you compare it to a pure benfotiamine bottle.
pros: Low 100 mg capsule suits small doses
cons: Needs several capsules for a larger dose
products.idealFor: Cautious first-time users who prefer a low dose and documentation.
products.skipIf: You want a high dose from few capsules.

products.name: Benfotiamine 600mg Per Serving, 180 Veggie Capsules (300mg Per Cap), Fat Soluble Vitamin B1
products.verdict: Pure benfotiamine at 300 mg per vegetable capsule, with outside lab testing and a long allergen-free list.
products.description:
DEAL Supplement packs 300 mg of benfotiamine into each of 180 vegetable capsules, so a 600 mg serving is 2 capsules and a bottle is a 90-day supply. It is vegan, made in the USA, third-party lab tested, and free of gluten, dairy, eggs, peanuts, soy, wheat and yeast.

It ranks fifth because the allergen list is the longest in the group and the dose per capsule is high, which suits people who dislike swallowing many pills. It sits behind Nutricost because the facility certification is less clear, and behind Double Wood because it cannot be split into smaller servings.

Buy it if you have food sensitivities and want a 600 mg serving. The caveat is that 300 mg capsules are large, and the dose is high enough that you should confirm it with your doctor first.
products.idealFor: People with food sensitivities who want a 600 mg serving.
products.skipIf: You prefer to start low and adjust.

products.name: Vitamin B1 Benfotiamine 600mg Per Serving, 240 Coconut Oil Softgels
products.verdict: A softgel with coconut oil and a 600 mg serving, for anyone who prefers oil-based delivery.
products.description:
Micro Ingredients sells 240 softgels with 3 softgels per serving to reach 600 mg of benfotiamine, so each softgel carries about 200 mg. The softgel includes coconut oil, avoids artificial colors and flavors, and is described as free of soy, dairy, gluten and preservatives, with third-party lab testing.

It ranks sixth because three softgels per serving is a lot to swallow and the supply works out to about 80 servings, below the 90 of the capsule bottles. The oil carrier is the appeal: for a fat soluble nutrient some people prefer a softgel to a dry capsule, though the listing does not publish data comparing absorption.

Buy it if you dislike dry capsules. The caveat is the softgel count, and the claims the listing makes about outcomes, which we do not repeat.
pros: Free of soy, dairy and gluten
products.idealFor: People who prefer oil-based softgels to dry capsules.
products.skipIf: You dislike swallowing several large softgels.

products.name: Nutri TTFD Thiamine B1 Supplement, 100mg with Magnesium, 60 Servings
products.verdict: TTFD at 100 mg per capsule, with 8 mg of elemental magnesium and third-party lab testing.
products.description:
This product uses TTFD (thiamine tetrahydrofurfuryl disulfide), a different fat soluble B1 form from benfotiamine, at 100 mg per capsule. Each capsule also has 8 mg of elemental magnesium from 100 mg of magnesium taurinate, and the maker says it is third party lab tested and free of fillers.

It ranks seventh only because TTFD is a narrower choice: the listing offers less dose flexibility and fewer independent sources than benfotiamine. Of the two TTFD products here it is clearer, stating the exact magnesium amount, which is why it sits above the Thiamax.

Buy it if you have a reason to prefer TTFD. The caveat is that the form is a minority choice with less published consumer information, so ask your clinician which form and dose are appropriate.
pros: TTFD form for those who prefer it
products.idealFor: Buyers who specifically want TTFD rather than benfotiamine.
products.skipIf: You want the most documented and common form.

products.name: Objective Nutrients Thiamax TTFD Thiamine B1 Supplement, 100mg with Magnesium, 60 Capsules
products.verdict: A 100 mg TTFD capsule that is small, made in the USA, and light on label detail.
products.description:
Thiamax contains 100 mg of TTFD with magnesium in extra-small capsules, 60 per bottle. The maker says it is made in the USA, non-GMO and third-party tested, and it sits in the under $30 bracket.

It ranks last because the listing gives no amount for the magnesium and spends most of its space on outcome claims, which we leave out. It beats nothing on documentation. Against the Nutri TTFD it is the same dose and the same count but less specific, and its small capsule is the one practical advantage.

Buy it if you want TTFD and find large capsules hard to swallow. The caveat is label clarity: read the Supplement Facts panel and do not rely on front-of-bottle promises.
products.idealFor: TTFD users who struggle with large capsules.
products.skipIf: You want exact ingredient amounts on the listing.

whatMatters.detail: Both are fat soluble forms of vitamin B1, but they are different molecules. Benfotiamine is the more common form, with more products to compare, while TTFD is a smaller niche. Check which form the Supplement Facts panel names, and ask your clinician which suits you, since the two are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

Per capsule and per serving are different numbers. Nutricost lists 600 mg per serving from two capsules, Double Wood 300 mg from two 150 mg capsules, and Micro Ingredients 600 mg from three softgels. Read the serving size line, then divide, before comparing bottles.

Supplements are not pre-approved by regulators the way drugs are, so independent testing matters. An NSF certified facility is a manufacturing credential, while lot testing and a certificate of analysis speak to each batch. Look for named testing, not just words like pure or clean.

A capsule is a dry powder in a shell, and a softgel suspends the ingredient in oil. Some people prefer oil with a fat soluble nutrient, but a listing is not evidence of better absorption. Choose on swallowing comfort, serving count and diet needs.

A bottle price means little until you divide by servings. Nutricost and DEAL Supplement give 90 servings, Double Wood and the TTFD products 60. Check the count and the serving size, and watch for products whose dose changes the days of supply.

faq.q: Can I take these with other medications or supplements?
faq.a: Speak to your doctor or pharmacist first. This is especially important with any prescription. Products such as Nutri TTFD add magnesium, and Life Extension combines two B1 forms, so check every label and avoid doubling up.

faq.q: What is the most common buying mistake?
faq.a: Comparing the big number on the front. Nutricost's 600 mg is a two-capsule serving, while Pure Encapsulations lists 200 mg per capsule. Always check the serving size and capsule count.

faq.q: Is benfotiamine worth it over regular thiamine?
faq.a: Benfotiamine is a fat soluble form that manufacturers describe as more absorbable than ordinary thiamine, but we cannot judge individual response. A clinician can say whether a fat soluble form makes sense for you.

Follow the label and your clinician's advice. Double Wood designs its 150 mg capsules to be divided between lunch and dinner. Taking a fat soluble product with a meal containing some fat is a common label suggestion.
Keep the bottle tightly closed, cool and dry, away from sun. A softgel such as Micro Ingredients can soften in heat, and capsules absorb moisture in a bathroom. Check the expiry date on every bottle.

faq.q: Are TTFD products the same as benfotiamine?
faq.a: No. TTFD, as in Nutri TTFD and Thiamax, is a different fat soluble B1 compound with a different dose range. Do not swap one for the other by milligram without clinician advice.

finalTake: Choose Pure Encapsulations BenfoMax for a clean single-ingredient label, Double Wood for a split-dose approach with testing for microbes and heavy metals, or Nutricost for a long, low-cost 600 mg supply from an NSF certified facility. Pick TTFD only if you have a specific reason. Whatever you buy, read the serving size line, ask your doctor first and do not rely on any outcome promise printed on a bottle.
